items.title: George Wein — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History
items.q: I booked everything in sight after that, everybody: Art Tatum, Billie Holiday, you name them... They all worked ... Louie Armstrong worked for me, Duke Ellington, and that's when I really learned my trade.

ctx.x: Now, you knew a couple of the musicians from having been out in the clubs in Boston.

I knew a musician called Frankie Newton. I don't know whether you knew Frankie. But Frankie was a wonderful trumpet player. He was on Billie Holiday's recording Strange Fruit. And he was more or less of a mentor to me because he indoctrinated me with a taste in music. For instance, I would hear J.C. Higginbotham, I loved dearly, and he would then tell me, Vic Dickenson is the man on trombone. Listen to him. And I'd listen and I'd hear the difference. And he loved to play with a mute and we'd work together. I'd…
me. The noise obliterates the music. It's too bad because some of the music isn't bad, but you can't get over that noise. It's very difficult.
